description: Solo developer tackling the 'Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots' challenge with PyroHarmonize. Using Python, ML cross-calibration, and spatiotemporal clustering to resolve the 20-year satellite resolution gap between MODIS and VIIRS. Synthesizing a unified, continuous 25-year Burning Activity Calendar to empower wildfire response and climate research with open NASA FIRMS data.
summary:
For over two decades, NASA satellites have been our eyes in the sky for tracking global wildfires. But in 2012, something tricky happened: NASA switched from the older MODIS satellite sensor (1 km resolution) to the newer, sharper VIIRS sensor (375 m). Overnight, recorded fire counts jumped by over 300%. The Earth didn't suddenly catch fire three times more—the new camera was simply picking up smaller flames and splitting single fires into multiple dots. This created a massive headache for scientists trying to compare historical fire records across decades.
I built PyroHarmonize to bridge this 20-year satellite gap. Using spatial clustering, the app groups scattered satellite dots back into real physical fire events. Then, an ML cross-calibration model trained on years where both satellites flew together smoothly normalizes fire intensity numbers.
The result is a continuous 25-year "Burning Activity Calendar" (2000–2025). Now, firefighters, forest managers, and climate scientists can finally track real climate shifts—like fire seasons lasting 12 days longer—without being misled by satellite upgrades.
details:
PyroHarmonize — Making 24 Years of Satellite Fire Data Comparable

An open-source scientific pipeline and web app combining satellite remote sensing, cross-sensor calibration with machine learning, and interactive geospatial analytics.

PyroHarmonize: one consistent fire record from MODIS to VIIRS

The problem

Since 2000, NASA has mapped active fires with MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and since 2012 with VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21). The sensors are not interchangeable. A MODIS pixel is about 1 km at nadir and grows toward the swath edge; a VIIRS I-band pixel is 375 m. VIIRS detects smaller and cooler fires and splits one fire front into many detections. In my northern California data, NOAA-20 VIIRS reports 8.8 times as many hot spots as Aqua MODIS over the same area and months. A naive switch of sensor would show a fire surge that never happened.

The timing makes this urgent. The Suomi-NPP fire data stream ended on 2 November 2026, and NASA plans to stop MODIS science data collection in 2027 (Terra in February, Aqua in September). The 24-year record must continue on NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 without a break in meaning.

What I built

An open-source pipeline and web app that puts every satellite on the Aqua MODIS scale and turns the result into a burning activity calendar (year x day of year). In the app you choose an area on the map and a period, and get the harmonised calendar, anomaly flags, fire-season timing, sensor diagnostics and CSV exports.

The live demo lets you switch between the three validated regions: northern California (November 2000 to December 2024), Portugal and northern Australia (April 2018 to December 2024): https://jeeson-kurian.github.io/pyro-harmonize/

Method

1. Data and coverage. NASA FIRMS standard-processing archive via the area API, with a manifest of every day requested and returned. Days outside coverage are missing, never zero. Quality control removes non-vegetation detections and low-confidence pixels and keeps the provenance of every row.

2. A common observation unit. Detections are mapped to 10 km equal-area cells and local solar half-days (day 06-18 h, night 18-06 h), with overpasses separated by time gaps. A cell is active for a platform if it reported at least one detection. Pixel count and FRP per overpass are kept as features. This removes the pixel-size effect at its source: eight VIIRS pixels on one front count once, like one MODIS pixel.

3. Cross-sensor calibration. VIIRS and Aqua are paired cell by cell on days both were observing. Candidate models range from no calibration and a constant ratio to a logistic detection model, P(Aqua reports the cell | VIIRS active), using log FRP, log pixel count, day/night and time of year, with a correction for cells only Aqua saw. FRP candidates include a log-log regression with Duan smearing and ridge regression.

4. Selection on unseen data. Every candidate is scored with leave-years-out cross-validation (5 folds over 7 years) on monthly totals, using scaled RMSE. The simplest method is kept unless a more complex one is more than 2 % better. A forward test (fit 2018-22, predict 2023-24) is reported separately. The 90 % band comes from out-of-fold monthly errors.

5. The record. Aqua where it observed; otherwise the mean of the calibrated VIIRS satellites, never their sum; Terra before Aqua's launch. Every day carries its source.

6. Analytics. Anomalies against the same month in all other years (percentile and robust z-score; "exceptional" needs both the 95th percentile and |z| >= 3). Fire-season start, peak and end from 10/50/90 % of each fire year's activity, trends with Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall, and no cause assigned.

Results on real NASA data

Three regions, two fire regimes: northern California (2000-2024), Portugal and the tropical savanna of northern Australia (2018-2024), about 2.96 million detections after quality control.

- Held-out years: the raw VIIRS-Aqua gap of +514 % to +781 % falls to within 2 % in every region (California +1.5 %, Portugal +0.1 %, Australia +0.1 %), with 6 to 14 % typical monthly error. One constant ratio leaves 47 % monthly error in California.

- MODIS switched off for 2023-24, calibration only on earlier years: the record continued from VIIRS alone stays within 7 % of what Aqua really observed (-6.0 %, +2.9 %, -6.3 %; rank correlation 0.93 to 0.99). This is the end-of-MODIS scenario, tested.

- Robustness: repeated for 2021-22, before Aqua's orbit drift, active cells stay within -8 % to +3 %. Results are stable for 5, 10 and 25 km cells.

- Observing-system check: from fire data alone, the pipeline measured Aqua's overpass drift (stable around 13:05-13:13 local solar time until 2022, 13:25 in 2023, 13:43 in 2024), consistent with NASA's documentation.

Limits, stated openly

Aqua is the reference, not ground truth. FRP converts well in the savanna but not in California or Portugal, where Aqua's drift is part of the cause. Each region needs its own calibration: a borrowed one leaves 22 to 55 % monthly error instead of 6 to 15 %. The California season-length trend over 23 fire years is not significant (p = 0.21), so I don't claim one.

Why it matters

Researchers, fire agencies and climate assessments get a long-term fire record that does not jump when the satellite changes, with its uncertainty quantified, ready for the post-MODIS era.

Engineering

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn), FastAPI and Uvicorn, Leaflet with Esri imagery. 72 automated tests including a blind reconstruction test, GitHub Actions CI, GitHub Pages demo, and one command to reproduce every report.
